$comment: One entry per fixture. Read by both the TypeScript and Rust test suites — see ../README.md.
GOVERNED BY ADR-0009 (strict import), which superseded ADR-0008's permissive tiers.
`outcome` IS DECIDED ENTIRELY BY THE LIBRARIES. A game errors when pgn-reader / shakmaty /
chessops refuse it, and otherwise it imports. We add no validation of our own — not a spec
checker, not a zero-moves guard, nothing. Fourteen of eighteen fixtures therefore IMPORT, several
of them despite not conforming to the PGN specification: duplicate tags, a Result disagreeing
with the termination marker, missing roster tags, an unterminated comment that eats four plies,
and bytes that are not PGN at all. Those are ADR-0009's ACCEPTED RISKS, listed in the ADR, and
each note says so. `errorCode` has only two values because that is all the libraries distinguish:
a move token they will not play, and a starting position they will not build.
TWO KINDS OF FIELD, and conflating them would make this corpus look verified when it is not.
SPECIFICATION, asserted by nothing yet: `outcome` and `errorCode` are what ADR-0009 requires of
the importer. B-007 asserts them; there is no importer today.
OBSERVED, asserted by mainline.test.ts today: `plies` and `truncatedAtPly` are measured from the
frontend reader. They describe DISPLAY behaviour and are unaffected by import policy.

fixtures.note: The negative control: conforms in every respect. A corpus that only held rejections would be passed by an importer that refuses everything.

ERRORS because the LIBRARY refuses the token — 4. Qg7 is well-formed SAN and illegal in the position reached, so parseSan returns nothing. That is the parser's decision, not a check of ours, and it is why this is one of only four errors in eighteen fixtures. The error detail must carry ply 6 and the token. Two further legal-looking moves follow deliberately: a parser that skipped rather than stopped would report the wrong ply.

IMPORTS, and this is the most uncomfortable entry in the corpus — an ACCEPTED RISK in ADR-0009, not an oversight. MEASURED: the unclosed `{` swallows moves 3 and 4 and the termination marker, and the parse reports complete SUCCESS with truncatedAtPly null. Four plies vanish with no signal whatsoever. Detecting it would mean doing our own brace matching, which is the validator ADR-0009 declines to write. Accepted because the file stays on disk and a wrong row costs a re-import (B-078).

IMPORTS, as two rows rather than one — MEASURED: the unclosed quote in [Event "...] runs on to the next quote, consuming the following tag lines, and the tokenizer treats the leftover movetext as a SEPARATE game with default headers. The library refuses nothing, so neither do we. Consequence for the error report: a game's index within a file is not a stable identifier, so identifying header text must travel with any error rather than the index alone.

IMPORTS with `?` values — an ACCEPTED RISK. MEASURED: chessops FILLS IN the five absent roster tags with defaults, Event becoming "?" and Result "*", so the header map always holds seven entries and a missing tag is indistinguishable from a tag whose value is literally "?". Telling them apart needs the bytes, which is a check we are not writing.

IMPORTS keeping the FIRST occurrence — an ACCEPTED RISK. Result appears twice (1-0 then 0-1) and Date twice; the specification requires tag names to be unique, and the library does not enforce it. MEASURED for chessops; **whether pgn-reader resolves the same way is unmeasured, and a difference would be a genuine B-064 divergence on a file neither library considers broken.** Document it, do not police it.

IMPORTS — an ACCEPTED RISK, and a reminder that 'derive hot fields from the tags' is not the whole story. The tag reads [Result "1-0"] and the movetext ends 0-1; MEASURED, chessops reports 0-1, so the termination marker silently overwrites the header. The derived `result` column can therefore disagree with the file's own tag, which ADR-0005 makes a re-import to fix rather than data loss.

IMPORTS as a row with no moves. A complete roster and no movetext, which the library accepts without complaint — so we accept it too. Refusing it would need a zero-moves rule of ours, and an earlier draft of ADR-0009 had exactly that before the owner pointed out it is still our validation wearing a smaller hat. It is also not obviously wrong: a scheduled-but-unplayed game legitimately looks like this.

IMPORTS as one junk row, and that is an ACCEPTED RISK rather than a gap. A PNG signature plus random bytes, named .pgn. MEASURED: the library does not throw and does not return zero games — it returns ONE game with seven default headers and no moves. So 'the parser returned a game' is not evidence that a game exists. We accept the junk row because rejecting it means writing our own check; it is visible, empty, and removable, and if it ever becomes annoying the targeted fix is one line plus this fixture (ADR-0009 says so explicitly).

IMPORTS, and it is the one deliberate tolerance in ADR-0009 — compliance rather than permissiveness, because the PGN specification names ISO 8859-1 while modern exporters emit UTF-8 and declare nothing. Try UTF-8, fall back to Latin-1, record which was used: two lines, and rejecting this file would mean rejecting a conforming one. Without the fallback the moves parse perfectly and the accented player names come back as U+FFFD, so the game looks fine and the people in it are quietly corrupted (B-058).

ERRORS, but NOT for the reason it looks like, and this fixture is the clearest statement of ADR-0009's accepted risk. MEASURED: 2. Sf3 (Springer, knight) is NOT refused — the tokenizer drops the unrecognised piece letter and yields `f3`, a legal pawn move, and likewise Sc6 -> c6. So plies 3 and 4 import as moves nobody played, and the game only errors when 3. Lb5 finally fails. **We do not detect the rewriting and we are not going to** — that was ADR-0008 rule 4 and B-098, both rejected. A German file that happened to reinterpret cleanly all the way through would import as a wrong game, silently. Accepted because the sources are chess.com and lichess, which emit English SAN. UNMEASURED and B-007 milestone 1: whether pgn-reader alters tokens the same way.

The same accepted risk through a different convention: 2. Cf3 (cavalier) becomes f3, Cc6 becomes c6, and 3. Fb5 is what finally fails. Two fixtures rather than one because the conventions use different letters, so an importer that special-cased German would pass one and fail the other.

IMPORTS as the rook move — and this fixture shows what strictness bought. White has Ke1 and Ra1, both able to reach d1, so `Rd1` is a legal rook move in English and a legal KING move in French; legality cannot arbitrate. ADR-0008 needed a rule and a heuristic file-wide language scan for this. Under ADR-0009 the question does not arise: the library reads English SAN, plays the rook, and the game imports. B-098 was rejected on the strength of this.

A legal Crazyhouse game imports normally — variants are selected, not refused. MEASURED: chessops's startingPosition() reads the Variant tag and returns a Crazyhouse position, so the mainline derives correctly, pocket visible in the FEN and `P@e4` played as a drop. shakmaty covers the same eight rule sets via VariantPosition behind its `variant` cargo feature; the difference is that it must be ASKED, which is the asymmetry behind ADR-0008's addendum.

ERRORS because the library refuses to build the start position: a Variant tag naming something neither implements ("Grand Chess") fails symmetrically — ParseVariantError in shakmaty, ERR_VARIANT in chessops. Both libraries distinguish that from a malformed FEN in their own error kinds, so the detail can carry the distinction without us inferring it. Worth keeping for what the frontend does: startingPosition() failing surfaces as truncatedAtPly 0, the same observable as a bad FEN.

IMPORTS a plausible wrong game — an ACCEPTED RISK, and the quietest failure in the corpus. MEASURED: [Variant "Fischerandom"] silently maps to STANDARD chess and the standard starting position, so a Chess960 game with no FEN header derives a mainline that is legal and wrong, reporting nothing. Catching it means checking variant names against a list we maintain, which is a rulebook. Accepted because real Chess960 exports carry SetUp/FEN — and 'normally' is doing the work in that sentence.

Both dedupe fixtures simply import, because there is no dedupe: ADR-0008's content key was removed from the MVP before ADR-0009 removed the rest. Kept as specification for B-022, whenever merging earns a customer. Ten tags, per-move { [%clk] } comments, movetext wrapped across three lines, LF endings.

The same game re-exported: seven tags, clock comments stripped, different wrapping, CRLF endings, marker on its own line. Byte-different in every respect a naive hash would notice, identical in players, event, date, round, result and moves. Importing both produces two rows — the expected MVP behaviour, worth a test so nobody 'fixes' it into a silent merge. Whenever B-022 keys on games, the key must include the variant.
